summary: The note surveys how construction and demolition (C&D) waste recycling is evolving, covering the scale of the problem, companies, AI sorting technology, recycled materials, partnerships, education, policy, local projects and international cooperation. It argues that recycling C&D waste is a necessary shift in building practice rather than a passing trend. Specific organizations, people and dates from late 2023 to 2024 illustrate each area.
one_line: Overview of innovative C&D waste recycling efforts in technology, industry, policy, education and community projects that turn construction debris into resources.
key_facts: A Sustainable Building Alliance report published October 15, 2023 said C&D waste accounted for approximately 35% of all waste generated in the United States.

EcoConstruct Solutions, led by CEO Rachel Goodman, began in late 2023 and believes almost 90% of construction site waste can be recycled or reused; it uses advanced sorting technologies and mobile recycling units deployed at construction sites.
On November 12, 2023, TechRecycle Inc. unveiled a patented machine that sorts mixed C&D waste with 98% accuracy.
Marcus Leland's company GreenRoads uses recycled aggregate from crushed concrete in road construction and had recycled over 1 million tons of concrete by March 1, 2024.

The National Construction Material Recycling Initiative (NCMRI) was launched on September 20, 2023, spearheaded by environmental advocate Olivia Sanchez, to unite construction firms, recyclers, suppliers and policymakers.
The Green Construction Academy, founded by James Chung on December 5, 2023, has certified over 10,000 individuals in sustainable construction and waste management.
The Sustainable Construction Materials Act, passed on January 15, 2024, imposes mandatory C&D recycling targets and subsidizes projects using a certain percentage of recycled content.
Policy strategist Andrew Kim said, "Legislation can serve as both a carrot and a stick."
The Denver Deconstruction Project, started February 22, 2024, promotes deconstructing rather than demolishing buildings and supplies low-cost materials for community housing projects.
The International Summit on Construction Recycling was held in Tokyo on August 17, 2024, with delegates from over 50 countries.
"Urban mining" treats buildings as material banks for future projects.
Recycled materials such as concrete, brick, wood, metal and glass are finding new applications.
